episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Repair Culture & Practical Tech
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Repair Culture & Practical Tech.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: What are we actually measuring?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Two vehicle MVI in 100 Mile House sent two to hospital and Search and Rescue teams find person who was lost over the weekend, plus 13 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: How should rural communities measure equipment repairability and reliability beyond standardized spec sheets and online review scores? Topics include: Limitations of spec sheets and online review scores for rural equipment decisions, Proxy metrics and how they can drift from measuring actual reliability to measuring repair speed, Local expertise and institutional knowledge versus centralized data sources, Network dependency and the cable-unplugged test for equipment resilience, Institutional sustainability of community-maintained repair logs and failure databases.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Boys and Girls Club of Williams Lake

discussion.central_question: How should rural communities measure equipment repairability and reliability beyond standardized spec sheets and online review scores?
discussion.riley_position: People should track practical repairability metrics like downtime, repair time, local repair expertise, and network dependency, sharing this data through community logs to build better local decision-making tools that account for regional failure patterns.
riley_key_evidence: iFixit's Apple Watch teardown shows no repairability improvement despite generations of iterations, revealing that headline scores can miss meaningful data
Commercial fleets already track hours down, dollars spent, and days to fix in detailed logs that provide actionable insights
Search and rescue teams and racing communities maintain real field failure databases from actual use under local conditions that beat magazine reviews
discussion.casey_position: While better personal metrics help attentive buyers, most people still purchase based on headlines and star ratings, so community logging efforts will struggle with maintenance and adoption unless embedded in existing institutional practices like volunteer organizations.
casey_key_evidence: Repair metrics can drift into false proxies—fast courier delivery makes days-to-fix look good while machines still fail repeatedly
Community sheets depend on a single maintainer while benefiting many readers, creating an unsustainable incentive gap
Most rural programs die when the enthusiast maintaining them moves away, suggesting standalone logging systems lack institutional resilience
discussion.resolution: They agreed to pilot a small experiment: a shared community spreadsheet tracking equipment failures, downtime, and repair time for local ranchers and backcountry users, with four columns, to test whether neighbors will actually contribute data and whether the practice survives beyond early adoption.
